hero.name: Jaya
hero.who: a homemaker in Vadodara who has lost and regained the same weight three times

story.b: Jaya is forty-seven and knows calorie counts by heart. Two rotis, about two hundred. A bowl of dal, around one fifty. Three times in six years she has eaten tiny portions, lost eight kilos and felt proud at a cousin's wedding. And three times the weight crept back within a year, along with constant hunger and a short temper. Now she is back where she started. At her last check-up, her doctor in Alkapuri mentioned that her blood sugar is borderline. Her daughter Hetal says she just needs more willpower. Jaya is not so sure. She has had plenty of willpower. It never seems to last.

ask.q: Jaya has lost and regained weight three times by eating less. What would be the wisest next step?
o: Eat even less this time, and push through the hunger
Talk with her doctor and look again at what and when she eats, not just how much
Give up, since her body is clearly just made this way
ask.why: Eating less has worked briefly and then failed three times, so doing more of it is unlikely to change the result. Her borderline sugar also makes it wise to guide any changes with her doctor. Giving up ignores that there may be approaches she has not yet tried.

chapters.take: If the same diet keeps failing, the approach may need to change, not your willpower.

story.b: Jaya tries a small experiment. On Monday, breakfast is white bread toast with jam and sweet tea. On Tuesday, she eats a moong dal chilla with some paneer and tea without sugar. On paper, the calories are about the same. But by eleven on Monday she is hungry and irritable, opening the biscuit tin. On Tuesday she does not think about food until lunch. She keeps a small diary for two weeks, noting what she ate and when hunger came back. The pattern surprises her. Meals heavy in sugar and white flour leave her hungry fast. Meals with protein, vegetables and some fat keep her steady for hours.

ask.q: Jaya's neighbour says a calorie is a calorie, so a jalebi breakfast equals a paneer one. What could Jaya share?
o: That she agrees, and only the total count matters
That jalebi is fine if she skips lunch to balance it
That similar calories can affect hunger very differently, as her own diary shows
ask.why: Her diary shows meals with similar calories leaving her full or hungry very differently, which fits the book's argument that hormones matter, not just counts. Treating all calories as equal ignores what she has seen herself, and skipping lunch to make up for jalebi often leads to more hunger later.

chapters.take: Same calories, different meals, different effects. Notice how food leaves you feeling.

story.h: Reading the back of the packet
story.b: At her next check-up, Jaya's doctor explains her borderline sugar in simple words. Her body may be starting to respond less well to insulin, and over the years that can move a person toward diabetes. He suggests some changes and a repeat test in three months. At home, Jaya looks at her kitchen with new eyes. The muesli her daughter bought for her diet, labelled healthy, has more sugar than she expected. So does the malt drink in the cupboard and the digestive biscuits she eats with tea. She starts turning every packet over at the supermarket on Race Course Road and reading the sugar line before it goes in the trolley.

ask.q: Hetal picks a fruit yoghurt marked healthy and low fat for her mother. What should Jaya do?
o: Trust the label, since healthy and low fat say enough
Check the sugar line on the back before buying
Buy two, since low fat means she can eat more
ask.why: Front labels are written to sell, while the sugar line on the back tells what is actually inside. Many low-fat products add sugar for taste, which matters for someone watching her blood sugar. Trusting the label, or eating more because of it, can quietly undo her efforts.

chapters.take: Read the sugar line, not the promise on the front of the packet.

story.b: One day Jaya counts how often she eats. Tea and two biscuits at six thirty. Breakfast at eight thirty. A banana at eleven. Lunch at one thirty. Chai with farsan at four thirty when the neighbours drop by. Dinner at eight thirty. A few dates at ten in front of the television. Seven times, and she had thought of herself as a light eater. So she decides to try three proper meals with nothing in between except water, plain tea or unsweetened buttermilk. The first week, four thirty is hard, especially when the neighbours bring dhokla. But by the third week, the evening hunger arrives later and feels gentler.

ask.q: When Jaya's neighbours bring snacks at four thirty, what is a good way to keep her new routine?
o: Join them with plain tea or water, and enjoy the company without the plate
Stop meeting the neighbours until the habit is set
Eat the snacks and skip dinner later to make up
ask.why: The aim is fewer eating occasions, not fewer friends. Plain tea lets her enjoy the visit while giving her body a real break between meals. Avoiding the neighbours makes the change lonely and hard to keep, and skipping dinner to balance snacks just moves the eating around.

chapters.take: Fewer eating times give the body real breaks between meals.

story.b: Jaya's sister-in-law tells her about a friend who did a three-day water fast and lost four kilos. Jaya is tempted, but her borderline sugar makes her nervous. At her next visit, she asks her doctor. He advises against long fasts for her, but says a longer gap between dinner and breakfast could be worth trying, as long as she watches how she feels and keeps up her follow-ups. So she moves dinner from eight thirty to seven fifteen, and has breakfast at eight. The family grumbles at first. Then her husband starts eating with her and says he sleeps better without a heavy late meal. Jaya finds the overnight gap easier than she feared.

ask.q: Jaya's friend, who takes diabetes medicine, wants to start fasting after reading about it. What should she do first?
o: Start with a long fast to see results quickly
Skip her medicine on fasting days to stay safe
Talk to her doctor before changing her eating pattern
ask.why: Fasting can interact with diabetes medicine, so any change needs a doctor's guidance. Skipping medicine without advice can be dangerous, and long fasts are not safe for everyone. A doctor can help her decide whether a gentle approach, like an earlier dinner, suits her at all.

chapters.take: Fasting may be a useful tool, but check with your doctor first.

story.b: The last big change is the hardest. Jaya loves khari biscuits with her tea, and her family loves sweets after dinner. She does not ban anything. Instead, she makes slow swaps. Khari for a handful of roasted peanuts. Sweet cold drinks at family lunches for chaas with jeera. White bread sandwiches for bajra rotla with vegetables. Sweets move from every night to Sundays only. She also notices that on nights she sleeps badly, or after a stressful phone call, she craves sugar more. So she starts a short evening walk in the society garden and switches off the television earlier.

ask.q: Hetal wants to help and suggests banning every sweet from the house forever. What approach would Jaya prefer?
o: A complete ban, starting today, with no exceptions
Gradual swaps away from sugar and refined flour, with sweets saved for occasions
No changes at all, since small swaps make no difference
ask.why: Steady swaps away from sugar and refined flour toward whole foods, protein and fibre are easier to keep for years than a strict ban. A sudden ban often leads to cravings and giving up. Doing nothing ignores how small daily changes can add up over time.

chapters.take: Slow swaps away from sugar and maida last longer than strict bans.

story.b: Three months later, Jaya goes back for her repeat test. Her doctor says her sugar reading has moved in the right direction, and asks her to keep going and keep checking in. She has lost a few kilos, more slowly than before, but this time she is not constantly hungry or snapping at everyone. Breakfast is usually a chilla or eggs. Four thirty is plain tea with the neighbours, who have started asking for her chaas recipe. Dinner is at seven fifteen, and the khari tin has been replaced by a jar of roasted peanuts. She no longer counts calories at every meal. She notices how food makes her feel, and she listens.

chapters.take: Lasting change comes from what and when you eat, guided by your doctor, not willpower alone.
